newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's CNMV cajoles companies into more openness.
newsitem.headline: Spain's CNMV cajoles companies into more openness.

text.p: Spain's stock market commission CNMV, eager to ensure the bourse is fit for the competition expected to follow Europe's single currency, is launching a campaign to educate companies on disclosing key information.

In the first of a series of informative letters, CNMV Chairman Juan Fernandez-Armesto wrote to listed companies, brokers and financial institutions on Tuesday on guidelines for revealing information that affects share prices.

While mandatory disclosure laws on sensitive share information have been on the books for some time, the CNMV in the past had tended to focus on companies' failure to stick to proper registration procedures and other formalities.
But it has bounded into action this year.

With the launch of the common currency just around the corner and Spain a likely contender, the CNMV is intent on transforming a market based on cosy ties into a transparent bourse that will be the market of choice for trade in Spanish companies.
Many European bourses are worried that the single currency could endanger their current niche in the domestic market, and are thus trying to improve standards.

The CNMV's guidelines gently suggest changes in the way many Spanish companies typically disclose information. They are likely to find resonance now that the CNMV has shown itself willing and able to penalise the cream of Spanish companies.
For example, at present many companies make official announcements of sensitive information during market hours, which run from 0800 GMT to 1300 GMT.
"The issuer should ensure, whenever possible, that the information be registered and made public with the market closed, in order to avoid distorsions in share prices.
Others often reveal key information to analysts at meetings or piecemeal to groups that then filters into the market before the entire market has been informed.
"All meetings with analysts, shareholders and investors or press conferences must be planned in advance to envisage questions whose answers might reveal confidential or sensitive information.
"The entity must abstain from revealing this type of information if it is not previously or simultaneously released to the market," Fernandez-Armesto wrote in the note.

The CNMV grabbed the market's attention last May, fining top utility Endesa and leading bank Banco Bilbao Vizcaya for failing to provide key information and for failing to keep key information confidential, respectively.

Both actions centred on 66.8 percent state-owned Endesa's controversial purchase late last year of regional utilities Sevillana de Electricidad and Fuerzas Electricas de Catalunya as it prepared for further privatisation.
Since these cases, mandatory disclosures of information to the CNMV have risen sharply as companies strive to come clean and adjust to Spain's new ethos of openness.
